o: Compare magnetic, optical and solid-state storage.
Justify storage choices using speed, capacity, durability and cost.
Explain why secondary storage is non-volatile.
r: Which type of memory is volatile: RAM or ROM?
RAM.
What does cache memory provide?
Faster access to frequently used data/instructions.
Convert 6,400 bits into bytes.
800 bytes.
Why does a saved file on an SSD remain after shutdown while unsaved RAM contents may not?
SSD is non-volatile secondary storage; RAM is volatile working memory.
c: Non-volatile storage
Secondary storage keeps saved files and programs without power.
Three technologies
Magnetic HDDs use magnetic patterns; optical discs use lasers; solid-state memory uses chips with no moving mechanical parts.
Comparison
Consider capacity, read/write speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost.
Justification
Link a stated feature of a device to the actual user requirement; no technology is always the best choice.

m.q: A travelling photographer needs to move large files quickly and often drops their bag. Choose a storage device.
st: Identify speed, portability and physical durability as priorities.
Recommend a portable SSD.
Explain that an SSD usually transfers large files quickly.
Explain why its lack of moving mechanical parts reduces risk of knock damage.
Mention that SSDs can cost more per GB than HDDs and backups are still needed.

w: Recommend storage for very large, low-cost school archives.
A magnetic HDD because high-capacity storage is usually economical per GB.
Recommend a small portable storage device for homework.
USB flash drive or portable SSD; solid-state, compact and portable.
Explain why an expensive fast SSD is not automatically the best solution for every use.
Some tasks prioritise price or capacity over speed; user needs determine choice.

k.q: Predict how many equal-sized files fit on a drive.
p: Explain one reason storage choice needs more than just file count.
k.a: 64 ÷ 8 = 8 files; after the change 64 ÷ 16 = 4 files. Other factors include speed, durability, portability, reliability and cost.

e: Name two technologies used for secondary storage. [2 marks]
Any two: magnetic, optical, solid state [1 each].
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of an SSD over a magnetic HDD for a portable laptop. [4 marks]
No moving parts [1] so better shock resistance [1]; typically higher cost per GB [1] so high capacity may cost more [1].
A school needs 10 TB for older files. Recommend a suitable device and justify using two characteristics. [4 marks]
Magnetic HDD [1], high capacity [1] and relatively low cost per GB [1], both supporting an archive workload [1].
v: Uses magnetic properties to record bits.
Uses laser light to read disc data.
Uses memory chips without moving read/write heads.
Non-volatile storage for saved files and programs.
x: An SSD requires a moving read/write head.

010.t: CPU Architecture, Registers and Fetch–Execute Cycle
o: Distinguish CPU's Control Unit and ALU.
State roles of PC, MAR, MDR and accumulator.
r: Which storage technology has no moving read/write head?
Solid-state.
Why is an HDD often chosen for a large archive?
Large capacity and relatively low cost per GB.
Why is RAM not used as permanent file storage?
RAM is volatile.
Justify solid-state storage for a laptop used on a bumpy bus.
Shock resistance due to no moving parts and generally fast access; important files still need backups.
c: CPU roles
The Control Unit coordinates operations and decodes instructions; the ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Registers
PC: next instruction address; MAR: address being accessed; MDR: transferred data/instruction; ACC: calculation result.
Kitchen memory aid
PC = recipe bookmark; MAR = shelf location; MDR = ingredient fetched; ACC = mixing bowl for results.
Instruction cycle
Fetch the instruction, decode it and execute it; then repeat. Cache keeps frequently used data and instructions close to the CPU.

m.q: Explain a fetch using the PC, MAR, MDR and the Control Unit.
st: The PC identifies the address of the next instruction.
The address is copied to MAR.
The requested instruction transfers from memory into MDR.
The PC updates to reference the next instruction in sequence.
The Control Unit decodes the fetched instruction; it can then be executed, possibly using the ALU.

w: Which register stores the next instruction's address?
Program Counter (PC).
Where is the address of the memory location being accessed stored?
Memory Address Register (MAR).
Which unit calculates a sum and where might the result be held?
ALU performs arithmetic; accumulator can hold the result.

k.q: Predict the output of a short arithmetic program.
p: State which CPU component performs arithmetic.
k.a: 12, then 16. The ALU performs arithmetic; code is not a hardware simulation.

e: State what MAR and MDR each store. [2 marks]
MAR: accessed address [1]; MDR: data or instruction being transferred [1].
Explain the role of the Program Counter when fetching an instruction. [2 marks]
PC stores address of next instruction [1], providing the location to fetch next [1].
Explain how the Control Unit, ALU and accumulator contribute to processing an addition instruction. [4 marks]
CU decodes/co-ordinates [1], controls the operation [1], ALU calculates [1], ACC may store the result [1].
v: Stores the address of a memory location being accessed.
Stores address of the next instruction.
x: MDR stores the address of the next instruction.

011.t: CPU Performance: Clock Speed, Cache and Cores
o: Explain how clock speed, cache and cores affect CPU performance.
Recognise why a faster clock is not always a faster task completion.
r: What does MAR store?
The accessed memory address.
Name the CPU component that performs arithmetic.
ALU.
What does the PC store?
Address of the next instruction.
Describe a fetch using PC, MAR and MDR.
PC supplies next instruction address; MAR holds accessed address; MDR holds fetched instruction/data.
c: Clock speed
Clock speed is measured in Hz: clock cycles per second. One cycle does not necessarily equal one instruction.
Cache size
Cache stores frequently needed information closer to the CPU, reducing time spent accessing RAM.
Core count
Multiple cores enable more work in parallel when software supports simultaneous tasks.
Overall comparison
Architecture and task type also affect performance; do not infer an absolute winner from one specification.

m.q: Compare CPU A (2 GHz, 4 cores, 4 MB cache) with B (3 GHz, 2 cores, 8 MB cache). Which is faster?
st: CPU B has the higher clock speed.
CPU A has more cores, which can help with suitably parallel work.
CPU B has more cache, potentially reducing RAM access.
Explain that workload and architecture determine real performance.
Conclude neither is automatically fastest for every task.

w: CPU C is 2 GHz and CPU D is 3 GHz. Identify which has a higher clock speed.
CPU D.
Explain a performance benefit of cache.
Frequently needed data can be accessed faster, reducing slower RAM access.
Give a scenario in which more CPU cores help.
An application using parallel threads or several programs running concurrently.

k.q: Predict the number of billions of clock cycles in two seconds.
p: Predict the number of billion cycles.
Explain why cycle count is not the number of executed instructions.
k.a: 6 billion cycles; then 12 billion. An instruction can require different numbers of clock cycles and architecture matters.

e: State two characteristics affecting CPU performance. [2 marks]
Any two from clock speed, cache size, number of cores [1 each].
Explain how a larger cache may improve performance. [2 marks]
Holds frequently used data/instructions near CPU [1], reducing slower RAM accesses [1].
Two CPUs both run at 2 GHz but one has twice as many cores. Explain why it may not always finish a task faster. [4 marks]
More parallel capacity [1]; only when software uses multiple threads [1]; single-threaded code cannot fully use extra cores [1]; other factors such as cache and architecture matter [1].
v: Number of CPU clock cycles per second.
Small, fast memory holding frequently used information.
CPU processing unit able to execute instructions.
Running work simultaneously using multiple processing units.
x: 3 GHz guarantees exactly three billion instructions every second.

o: Explain why virtual memory may be needed.
Describe moving data between RAM and secondary storage.
Explain the performance cost of excessive swapping.
r: Explain one difference between RAM and ROM.
RAM is volatile working memory. ROM is non-volatile and commonly stores firmware.
A 300 × 100 bitmap uses four bits per pixel. Calculate its raw pixel-data size in bytes.
Why is lossless compression suitable for program files?
The exact original instructions must be recovered; lost or changed characters could break the program.
Explain why the CPU benefits from cache memory but cannot use a small cache as a complete replacement for main RAM.
Cache is very fast but small; it holds frequently needed data/instructions. RAM has much greater capacity for active programs and data.
c: When RAM is insufficient
The operating system can use part of secondary storage as virtual memory.
Data moves between locations
Inactive pages of a program can be stored on secondary storage so RAM can hold data needed now.
Virtual memory is slower
SSDs/HDDs have much slower access than RAM, so swapping can slow a computer.
A common misunderstanding
Virtual memory is not extra physical RAM. It allows the system to use secondary storage when needed.
Context
Too many open applications can cause heavy swapping and poor responsiveness.

m.q: A computer has 4 GB RAM but the active programs need 6 GB. What happens?
st: Compare required memory 6 GB with available RAM 4 GB.
The deficit is 6 − 4 = 2 GB.
Operating system moves some less-needed memory pages to secondary storage.
When those pages are required, the system transfers data back, possibly moving other pages out.
Repeated transfers slow performance because secondary storage is slower than RAM.

w: Where is virtual memory stored?
In part of secondary storage such as an SSD or HDD.
Why does heavy swapping slow a computer?
Data is being transferred between RAM and slower secondary storage.
Does virtual memory increase the amount of installed RAM?
No. It uses secondary storage as an extension of available memory.

k.q: Model a memory shortfall with arithmetic.
p: Predict the required extra capacity in GB.
Write a line to print zero when sufficient RAM is available (no IF needed: choose a suitable value).
k.a: 2 GB shortfall initially; 1 GB when ram = 5; choose required = 4, ram = 4 and the subtraction prints 0. This is a simple capacity model, not a simulation of virtual memory.

e: Define virtual memory. [2]
Part of secondary storage temporarily used to hold data/instructions when RAM is insufficient.
Describe the movement of data when RAM becomes full. [3]
Less-used data/pages move from RAM to secondary storage; required pages return to RAM when needed; this frees RAM for active processes.
Explain a possible effect of virtual memory on performance. [2]
Slower disk/SSD access and frequent swapping can delay program execution compared with RAM.
v: Secondary storage used as an extension when RAM is insufficient.
A unit of memory data moved between RAM and backing storage.
Transfer memory data between RAM and secondary storage.
Non-volatile storage such as an SSD or HDD.
x: Virtual memory usually operates at the same speed as physical RAM.

o: Explain why secondary storage is needed.
Compare magnetic, optical and solid-state technologies.
r: Why can using virtual memory make a computer slower?
Data must be moved between RAM and slower secondary storage; frequent swapping causes delays.
State one difference between RAM and ROM.
RAM is volatile/read-write working memory; ROM is non-volatile firmware storage.
State one advantage of Unicode over ASCII.
It can represent many more characters from different scripts.
A computer has 4 GB of RAM, but its active applications require 7 GB. Explain how the computer may continue running and why performance could decrease.
There is a 3 GB shortfall. The OS may use secondary storage as virtual memory, moving pages between RAM and storage; this is slower than accessing RAM.
c: Why secondary storage exists
It preserves programs, files and data after power is removed.
Magnetic
Hard disk drives offer large capacity at relatively low price per GB; moving parts make them vulnerable to knocks.
Optical
CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs use lasers; portable/removable, often slower and lower capacity than SSDs/HDDs.
Solid state
SSDs and flash drives have no moving parts, fast access and good portability, typically at a higher price per GB than HDDs.
Compare in context
OCR asks about capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost.

m.q: A film-editing workstation needs fast storage for active files and cheap capacity for archives.
st: Identify need one: fast access to current large video files.
Recommend SSD for working projects: high access speed and no moving parts.
Identify need two: lots of long-term storage on a budget.
Recommend HDD for archives: often lower cost per GB for large capacities.
Explain that either must be backed up; the storage type does not guarantee data safety.

w: Name one magnetic storage device.
Hard disk drive (HDD).
Name one optical storage medium.
DVD, CD or Blu-ray.
Why is an SSD often suitable for a laptop?
Fast, durable against knocks, and no moving parts.

k.q: Calculate how many files fit into a drive.
p: Predict how many equal-sized files fit.
Explain why storage capacity alone does not tell us which drive is best.
k.a: 5 files initially; 4 files when fileSize = 250. Speed, durability, reliability, portability and cost also matter. Units must match.

e: Name three technologies used for secondary storage. [3]
Magnetic, optical, solid state.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of an SSD compared with an HDD. [4]
Advantage: faster access / more resistant to shocks because no moving parts. Disadvantage: commonly higher purchase cost per GB.
Justify a suitable storage device for a school’s high-capacity, low-cost backup. [3]
HDD: large capacity and lower cost per GB; suitable for backups where maximum speed is less important.
v: Stores bits through magnetic properties, e.g. HDD.
Uses a laser to access disc data, e.g. DVD.
Stores bits electronically with no moving parts, e.g. SSD.
x: An HDD generally has no moving mechanical parts.
